result:
The library near my childhood home had a clock that ran seven minutes slow. Nobody fixed it for years. The librarians knew, the regulars knew, and eventually I learned to subtract seven minutes in my head whenever I glanced up from a book.

One summer, the clock disappeared. A week later it returned, freshly repaired and showing the correct time. I found this oddly disappointing. The slow clock had felt like a small secret the building shared with anyone who stayed long enough.

I still think about it sometimes when I see a sign with a letter missing or a tree growing around an old fence. Not everything imperfect is worth preserving. But some imperfections give us a way to recognize a place as our own.
